# Webhook Relay

Webhook Relay delivers application events to customer HTTPS endpoints with signed payloads, automatic retries, and delivery tracking. It runs as an Effect-based worker backed by PostgreSQL.

## Get started

From the repository root, install dependencies and start the local database:

```sh
pnpm install
 docker compose up -d postgres
```

Create the worker configuration:

```sh
cp packages/webhook-relay/.env.example packages/webhook-relay/.env
```

Set `DATABASE_URL` and `WEBHOOK_SIGNING_SECRET` in that file, then initialize and start the worker:

```sh
pnpm --filter @harbor/webhook-relay db:migrate
pnpm --filter @harbor/webhook-relay dev
```

Publish a sample event from another terminal:

```sh
pnpm --filter @harbor/webhook-relay send --url https://webhook.site/your-token --event invoice.paid
```

The command prints a delivery ID. Use `pnpm --filter @harbor/webhook-relay status <delivery-id>` to check its result.

## Worker internals and operations

The intake service validates each event before inserting a delivery row. It stores the serialized body rather than reconstructing it later so that signatures remain stable across retries.

The scheduler polls the delivery table every 500 milliseconds. Each poll selects at most 100 eligible rows ordered by their next attempt time and creation time.

Rows are claimed with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`. The claim transaction sets a lease owner and lease expiry before releasing its database connection.

Lease ownership is independent of the worker process ID. Each worker generates a random owner token at startup and includes that token in every completion update.

The dispatcher maintains a global concurrency limit of 32 deliveries. A separate per-host semaphore limits any single destination host to four active requests.

The request body is signed with HMAC-SHA256. The signature input contains the timestamp, a period separator, and the exact stored payload bytes.

Connection establishment has a three-second timeout. The complete request has a ten-second timeout, including response body draining.

Successful responses are any status from 200 through 299. Redirects are not followed because forwarding signed payloads could disclose event data to another destination.

Timeouts, connection failures, and server errors schedule another attempt. Most client errors mark the delivery as permanently failed, except for rate-limit responses.

Retry delays use exponential backoff with jitter. The scheduler persists the chosen delay so restarting a worker does not recalculate the next attempt time.

A lease sweeper runs every 30 seconds. It returns expired claims to the pending state and records a lease-expired attempt entry for later investigation.

During shutdown, the worker stops polling before interrupting its dispatch fibers. It allows in-flight requests five seconds to complete before releasing their claims.

Operators should compare pending delivery age with lease expiry counts before increasing concurrency. A growing queue with stable request latency usually indicates insufficient worker capacity.

If expired leases increase while database latency is high, first inspect connection pool saturation. Adding workers in that situation can increase contention and delay completion updates further.

Replay operations retain the original event ID but create a new delivery ID. This distinction lets operators trace repeated sends without overwriting the original delivery history.

## More documentation

See the [payload reference](../../docs/webhooks/payloads.md) for event schemas and the [command reference](../../docs/webhooks/cli.md) for CLI options.
